text: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your Agent SDK agent resolves returns, billing, and account issues through MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). To enforce identity checks, the team set `tool_choice` to force `get_customer` on the first turn of each session. An audit finds refunds issued to a second account that a customer raised mid-conversation and that was never verified. What change closes this gap?
options: Add a `PostToolUse` hook on `process_refund` that compares the refunded account against verified IDs and opens a reversal ticket when they differ
Add a `PreToolUse` hook that denies `process_refund` unless the target account ID matches one that `get_customer` verified in this session
Force `get_customer` with `tool_choice` on every turn instead of only the first, so verification runs before each new request is handled
Expand the `process_refund` description to state that the account must be verified by `get_customer` earlier in the same conversation
correct_answer: Add a `PreToolUse` hook that denies `process_refund` unless the target account ID matches one that `get_customer` verified in this session
explanation: Task 1.4 calls for a programmatic prerequisite that blocks a downstream tool until the prerequisite step has produced a verified result. A `PreToolUse` hook that checks the refund's target account against the IDs `get_customer` verified in this session blocks the call before money moves. Forcing `get_customer` on every turn makes a verification call happen, but nothing ties the later refund to the account that was verified, and it adds a tool call to every turn. A `PostToolUse` hook runs after the refund has already been issued, so it can only clean up. A description change is prompt-based guidance with a non-zero failure rate.

text: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your Agent SDK agent resolves returns, billing, and account issues through MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). `lookup_order` returns `created` as a Unix timestamp, the shipping server returns ISO 8601 dates, and the returns system uses numeric status codes such as `3`. The agent sometimes tells customers their return window has closed when it has not. The backend teams cannot change their APIs this quarter. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Add a table to the system prompt that explains each timestamp format and status code, so the agent converts them before reasoning about dates
Add a `PreToolUse` hook that rewrites each tool's input arguments into one shared date format before the call reaches the backend
Add few-shot examples showing correct return-window calculations from each of the three source formats, including the numeric status codes
Add a `PostToolUse` hook that converts every timestamp to ISO 8601 and maps status codes to labels before results reach the model
correct_answer: Add a `PostToolUse` hook that converts every timestamp to ISO 8601 and maps status codes to labels before results reach the model
explanation: Task 1.5 describes `PostToolUse` hooks that normalize heterogeneous data formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601, numeric status codes) from different MCP tools before the agent processes them. The conversion happens in code, so the model always reasons over one consistent format. A `PreToolUse` hook changes the request arguments, not the mixed formats coming back in the results. A system-prompt table and few-shot examples both ask the model to do the conversion itself, which is probabilistic and is exactly where the date errors come from.

text: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your Agent SDK agent resolves returns, billing, and account issues through MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). A customer's single message disputes a duplicate charge, asks where a delayed package is, and requests a refund on a damaged item above the agent's authority. The agent answers only the billing question, then escalates the refund. The human who picks it up has no access to the conversation transcript. Which TWO changes should you make?
options: Split the message into three items and investigate each before one combined reply, and escalate with a structured summary of customer ID, root cause, amount, and recommended action
Route the three concerns to parallel subagents that each reply to the customer separately, and include the last ten conversation turns verbatim in the escalation ticket
Split the message into three items and investigate each before one combined reply, and call `escalate_to_human` with a short note asking the human to contact the customer
Answer the first concern, then ask the customer to resend the other two as new messages, and escalate with a structured summary of ID, cause, amount, and action
correct_answer: Split the message into three items and investigate each before one combined reply, and escalate with a structured summary of customer ID, root cause, amount, and recommended action
explanation: Task 1.4 covers both halves. The agent should decompose a multi-concern request into distinct items, investigate each using shared context, and synthesize one unified resolution. When it escalates, the human lacks the transcript, so the handoff must be a structured summary with the customer ID, root cause, refund amount, and recommended action. Separate replies from parallel subagents fragment the answer, and pasting raw turns makes the human reconstruct the case. A short "please contact the customer" note gives the human nothing to act on. Asking the customer to resend their other concerns pushes the decomposition work back onto the customer.

text: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your Agent SDK agent resolves returns, billing, and account issues through MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). When `process_refund` rejects a refund because the item is outside the 30-day return policy, the MCP server returns `isError: true` with `errorCategory: "transient"`. The agent retries three times, then tells the customer the system is down and to try again tomorrow. How should the tool response change?
options: Keep `errorCategory: "transient"` but lower the agent's retry limit to one attempt, so the customer gets an answer faster after the first failure
Return `isError: false` with an empty result, so the agent treats the refund as declined and moves on without retrying the request
Mark it as a business-rule violation with `isRetryable: false` and a customer-friendly reason, so the agent explains the policy instead of retrying
Return `errorCategory: "permission"` with `isRetryable: true`, so the agent escalates to a human who has authority to approve the late refund
correct_answer: Mark it as a business-rule violation with `isRetryable: false` and a customer-friendly reason, so the agent explains the policy instead of retrying
explanation: Task 2.2 distinguishes transient, validation, permission, and business-rule errors. A policy rejection is a business-rule violation. It should carry `isRetryable: false` and a customer-friendly explanation, so the agent tells the customer about the 30-day policy instead of retrying. Mislabeling it as transient, even with fewer retries, still makes the agent report an outage that did not happen. Returning an empty success hides the failure from the agent. Labeling it as a retryable permission error misstates the cause, and an out-of-policy return is not a gap that a human must fill.

text: Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Your Agent SDK agent resolves returns, billing, and account issues through MCP tools (`get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, `escalate_to_human`). A caller gives only the name "Maria Lopez" and asks to cancel her latest order. `get_customer` returns three customer records with that name in different cities. Logs show the agent picks the record with the most recent order and cancels it, which was wrong in about a third of similar cases. What should the agent do instead?
options: Ask the customer for an additional identifier, such as email or order number, before choosing a record or calling any order tool
Escalate to a human whenever `get_customer` returns more than one record, since matching customers is outside the agent's authority
Choose the record whose city matches the caller's phone area code, and confirm the order details with the customer before cancelling it
Show the customer all three records with their addresses and order histories, and let the customer pick which account is theirs
correct_answer: Ask the customer for an additional identifier, such as email or order number, before choosing a record or calling any order tool
explanation: Task 5.2 says that when tool results return multiple matches, the agent should ask for additional identifiers rather than select a record based on heuristics. An area-code match is still a heuristic, and confirming order details afterward can leak another customer's data. Showing all three records exposes other customers' personal information. Escalating every multiple match lowers first-contact resolution when one more identifier resolves the ambiguity.

text: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your Agent SDK agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases with the built-in tools and MCP servers. An engineer asks it to "add comprehensive tests to the legacy billing service," which has 300 files and almost no tests. The workflow is a fixed chain: list files alphabetically, write tests for each in order, then run the suite. After two hours it has tested utility helpers but not the payment logic. Which decomposition fits this task?
options: Keep the fixed chain but sort the files by size, so the largest modules, which usually hold the core logic, are tested first
Split the file list evenly across ten parallel subagents that each write tests for thirty files, then merge their test files at the end
First map the structure and dependencies to find high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adds subtasks as dependencies are discovered
Use a per-file pass for each module followed by a cross-file integration pass, the same chain used for large pull request reviews
correct_answer: First map the structure and dependencies to find high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adds subtasks as dependencies are discovered
explanation: Task 1.6 separates predictable multi-aspect work, where a fixed prompt chain fits, from open-ended work like adding tests to a legacy codebase. For open-ended work, the agent first maps the structure, identifies high-impact areas, and creates a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies appear. Sorting by size is still a fixed order based on a guess. Ten parallel subagents cover files faster but still spend effort evenly instead of by impact. The per-file plus integration pattern is designed for reviewing a known set of changed files, not for deciding where testing effort matters.

text: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your Agent SDK agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases with the built-in tools and MCP servers. Last week an engineer ran a named session, `auth-audit`, that read 60 files in the auth module. Since then, a rebase rewrote most of those files and moved several into a new package. The engineer wants to continue the audit today. Which approach is most reliable?
options: Run `--resume auth-audit` and list the files the rebase changed, so the agent re-reads only those files and keeps the rest of its earlier analysis
Start a new session and inject a structured summary of last week's findings, letting the agent re-read the current files as it needs them
Use `fork_session` from `auth-audit` so the stale analysis stays in the original branch while the fork re-explores the rebased files
Run `--resume auth-audit` and then `/compact`, so the older tool results are condensed before the agent continues with the audit
correct_answer: Start a new session and inject a structured summary of last week's findings, letting the agent re-read the current files as it needs them
explanation: Task 1.7 says to resume when prior context is mostly valid, and to start fresh with an injected summary when prior tool results are stale. Here most of the files changed, so most of the session's tool results describe code that no longer exists. Listing changed files is the right move when only a few files changed, but here it would cover almost everything. A fork copies the same stale history into the new branch. `/compact` condenses the stale results instead of removing them, so the summary still describes the old code.

text: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your Agent SDK agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases with the built-in tools and MCP servers. The agent must rename the config key `retryLimit` to `maxRetries`. It first needs every file that references the key. It must then update `settings.ts`, where the identical line `retryLimit: 3,` appears in four different objects, and Edit fails each time with a non-unique match error. Which tool sequence is most reliable?
options: Use Glob with the pattern `**/*retryLimit*` to find references, then retry Edit on `settings.ts` with the same anchor text until it succeeds
Use Read on every file in the repository to find references, then retry Edit on `settings.ts` once for each of the four duplicate lines
Use Grep to find references, then use Glob to locate `settings.ts` and Write a new file containing only the four changed lines
Use Grep to find files containing `retryLimit`, then Read `settings.ts` in full and Write the whole updated file back
correct_answer: Use Grep to find files containing `retryLimit`, then Read `settings.ts` in full and Write the whole updated file back
explanation: Task 2.5 assigns Grep to content search (finding every file that mentions a name) and Glob to file-name patterns. When Edit cannot find unique anchor text, the reliable fallback is to Read the full file and Write the complete updated version. Glob matches file names, so `**/*retryLimit*` misses files that only mention the key in their contents. Reading every file up front is the opposite of building understanding incrementally. Repeating Edit with the same non-unique anchor fails the same way. Writing a file that contains only the changed lines destroys the rest of `settings.ts`.

text: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your Agent SDK agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases with the built-in tools and MCP servers. Your team added an internal MCP server with a `search_runbooks` tool described as "Searches runbooks." The agent ignores it and runs Grep across the repository, missing runbooks stored outside the repo. Each session also starts with several exploratory calls just to learn which runbook collections exist. What change addresses both problems?
options: Expand the tool description to explain its coverage and outputs beyond the repository, and expose the runbook catalog as an MCP resource
Remove Grep from the agent's allowed tools so it has to use `search_runbooks`, and add a `list_collections` tool for the agent to call first
Add a system prompt rule telling the agent to prefer MCP tools over built-in tools, and cache the collection names in a CLAUDE.md file
Move the server from user-scoped `~/.claude.json` to project-scoped `.mcp.json`, and add example runbook queries to the system prompt
correct_answer: Expand the tool description to explain its coverage and outputs beyond the repository, and expose the runbook catalog as an MCP resource
explanation: Task 2.4 covers both fixes. Enhancing an MCP tool's description to explain its capabilities and outputs prevents the agent from preferring a built-in tool like Grep. Exposing a content catalog as an MCP resource gives the agent visibility into what exists without exploratory tool calls. Removing Grep breaks every legitimate code search, and a `list_collections` tool is still an exploratory call. A blanket "prefer MCP tools" rule is keyword-sensitive guidance that overrides judgment, and a hand-maintained list in CLAUDE.md goes stale. The server is already connected, so changing its scope does not change which tool the agent picks.

text: Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. Your Agent SDK agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases with the built-in tools and MCP servers. It is mapping a 2,000-file monorepo over a multi-hour session. Late in the session it describes "the typical service pattern" instead of the specific classes it found earlier, and its answers contradict earlier findings. The next phase requires tracing three separate flows in depth. Which TWO changes best address this?
options: Switch to a model with a larger context window, and have the main agent trace all three flows itself so its findings stay in one place
Run `/compact` after each flow is traced, and rely on the compacted summary to carry the specific class names into the next phase
Record key findings in a scratchpad file the agent rereads, and delegate each flow to an Explore subagent that returns a summary
Record key findings in a scratchpad file the agent rereads, and start each flow trace by re-reading every file it already explored
correct_answer: Record key findings in a scratchpad file the agent rereads, and delegate each flow to an Explore subagent that returns a summary
explanation: Task 5.4 names this symptom: in extended sessions, models start referencing "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes discovered earlier. Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries, and delegating verbose discovery to Explore subagents keeps the main context focused on coordination. A larger window delays degradation but keeps all three verbose traces in one context. `/compact` helps when context fills, but a compacted summary is exactly where specific class names get lost. Re-reading every explored file refills the context with the verbose output that caused the problem.

text: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline runs Claude Code on pull requests to post review feedback and generate tests. A security step runs `claude -p` and must fail the build when any finding is critical. The gate script searches the text output for the word "critical," so it fails builds whose review says "no critical issues found." Last week it also passed a build whose review said "severe: SQL injection." What should you change?
options: Add a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to print `PASS` or `FAIL` on the last line of its output, and have the gate script read only that line
Gate on the exit code of `claude -p` instead of its text, since the command returns a non-zero status when the review reports a problem
Ask for JSON in the prompt, and have the gate script extract the text between the first and last curly braces before checking severities
Add `--output-format json` with a `--json-schema` whose severity field is an enum, and fail the build when any parsed finding is `critical`
correct_answer: Add `--output-format json` with a `--json-schema` whose severity field is an enum, and fail the build when any parsed finding is `critical`
explanation: Task 3.6 pairs `-p` with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` to produce machine-parseable structured findings in CI. A severity enum in the schema means the gate checks a field value instead of searching prose, so "no critical issues" cannot trip it and "severe" cannot slip past it. text: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline runs Claude Code on pull requests to post review feedback and generate tests. Developers also want to run the CI security checklist locally with `/security-review <path>`. The command file lives in one engineer's `~/.claude/commands/`. Teammates who copied it often run it without a path, so it reviews the whole repository and times out. How should you set this up?
options: Have each developer copy the file into their own `~/.claude/commands/`, and add a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to ask for a path first
Move the file to the repository's `.claude/commands/`, and add `argument-hint` frontmatter so developers are prompted for the path to review
Move the file to the repository's `.claude/commands/`, and add `allowed-tools` frontmatter limited to Read and Grep so full-repository reviews finish faster
Convert the checklist into a `.claude/rules/security.md` file with `paths: ["**/*"]`, so it loads automatically whenever any file in the repository is edited
correct_answer: Move the file to the repository's `.claude/commands/`, and add `argument-hint` frontmatter so developers are prompted for the path to review
explanation: Task 3.2 puts team-wide commands in the project's `.claude/commands/`, shared through version control, while `~/.claude/commands/` is personal. The `argument-hint` frontmatter prompts developers for the required parameter when they invoke the command. Per-user copies drift from the team version, and a CLAUDE.md instruction is guidance rather than an input prompt. Restricting `allowed-tools` limits what the command can do but does not supply the missing path. A path-scoped rule loads conventions while editing files; it does not run an on-demand review.

text: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline runs Claude Code on pull requests to post review feedback and generate tests. Developers are ignoring the generated tests. Many repeat scenarios the suite already covers, others test trivial getters, and several import a `mockDb` fixture that does not exist instead of the team's real `testDb` fixture. The test step receives only the diff. Which TWO changes address these problems?
options: Provide the existing test files in context for the test step, and raise its temperature so it proposes more varied and less obvious scenarios
List the existing test file names in the prompt, and add a `PostToolUse` hook that deletes any generated test importing an unknown fixture
Provide the existing test files in context for the test step, and document testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md
Ask for at most three tests per change to cut low-value output, and document testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md
correct_answer: Provide the existing test files in context for the test step, and document testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md
explanation: Task 3.6 covers both fixes. Providing existing test files in context lets test generation avoid scenarios the suite already covers. Documenting testing standards, what makes a test valuable, and the available fixtures in CLAUDE.md, which CI-invoked Claude Code reads, improves quality and stops invented fixtures. Higher temperature makes suggestions more varied, not less redundant. File names alone do not show which scenarios the tests cover, and deleting bad tests after generation hides the problem instead of preventing it. A hard cap on test count removes good tests along with poor ones and does nothing about duplicates.

text: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline runs Claude Code on pull requests to post review feedback and generate tests. A test-generation run on the `pricing` module produced three problems. The tests mock the tax service with the wrong interface, the same wrong mock makes the discount tests fail, and test names ignore the team's naming convention. The engineer is preparing follow-up prompts. What is the most effective way to send the feedback?
options: Describe the mock and discount failures together in one detailed message since they interact, and address the naming convention separately
Send all three issues in one message so Claude sees every problem at once, and attach the full failing test output for each of them
Fix the issues one at a time, starting with the naming convention because it is simplest, then the discount tests, then the tax mock
Rewrite the original prompt from scratch with all three requirements added, and rerun the generation in a fresh session
correct_answer: Describe the mock and discount failures together in one detailed message since they interact, and address the naming convention separately
explanation: Task 3.5 says to address interacting problems in a single detailed message, and to fix independent problems sequentially. The wrong mock causes the discount failures, so those two belong together. The naming convention is independent, so it can be handled on its own. Bundling the unrelated naming issue with the interacting pair dilutes the feedback. Fixing the discount tests before the mock means fixing a symptom. Starting over throws away the work that was correct and gives Claude no specific failures to iterate on.

text: Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Your pipeline runs Claude Code on pull requests to post review feedback and generate tests. For failing builds, the same Claude Code session that writes a fix also reviews that fix before the job opens a PR. The self-review approves subtle bugs, such as an off-by-one error, that a human reviewer catches in seconds. What change most improves the review's ability to catch these issues?
options: Enable extended thinking for the review step, so the same session reasons more deeply about its own fix before approving the change
Add a review instruction telling Claude to be skeptical of its own code and to list at least three possible defects before approving
Run the review step twice in the same session, and approve the fix only when both review passes agree that it is correct
Run the review in a separate Claude Code invocation that receives only the diff and tests, without the generator's reasoning context
correct_answer: Run the review in a separate Claude Code invocation that receives only the diff and tests, without the generator's reasoning context
explanation: Task 4.6 explains that a model reviewing its own work in the same session keeps the reasoning that produced it, so it is less likely to question it. An independent instance without that context catches subtle issues more effectively than self-review instructions or extended thinking. Extended thinking and a skepticism instruction both leave the generator's reasoning in place. A second pass in the same session repeats the same blind spot, so agreement between the two passes adds little.

text: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system extracts fields from unstructured documents with `tool_use` and JSON schemas for downstream systems. Your purchase-order schema marks `delivery_date` and `cost_center` as required strings, and `payment_terms` as an enum of `net30`, `net60`, or `prepaid`. Audits find plausible delivery dates and cost centers on orders that never stated them, and "2/10 net 30" terms forced into `net30`. Which schema change addresses both findings?
options: Keep the fields required, and add a prompt instruction telling Claude to enter "N/A" whenever a value does not appear in the document
Make `delivery_date` and `cost_center` nullable, and add `other` to the terms enum with a `payment_terms_detail` string for unlisted terms
Remove `delivery_date` and `cost_center` from the schema, and extract them in a second free-text pass that a human reviewer checks
Keep the fields required, add `"2/10 net 30"` to the enum, and add few-shot examples showing correct extraction of delivery dates
correct_answer: Make `delivery_date` and `cost_center` nullable, and add `other` to the terms enum with a `payment_terms_detail` string for unlisted terms
explanation: Task 4.3 says to make fields nullable when source documents may not contain the information, so the model is not pushed to fabricate values to satisfy a required field. It also recommends an `"other"` enum value plus a detail string for extensible categories. An "N/A" placeholder in a required string mixes a sentinel into real data, and downstream systems cannot tell it from a value. Moving the fields to a free-text pass gives up schema enforcement. Adding one more enum value fixes this case but not the next unlisted term, and few-shot examples do not remove the pressure a required field creates.

text: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system extracts fields from unstructured documents with `tool_use` and JSON schemas for downstream systems. Documents arrive as invoices, receipts, or contracts, and you define one extraction tool per type. With `tool_choice: "auto"`, about 5% of responses are prose summaries with no tool call. A separate workflow must run `extract_metadata` before any enrichment tool on the same document. Which configuration fits both workflows?
options: Force `extract_invoice` by name for the mixed workflow because invoices are the most common type, and use `tool_choice: "any"` for the metadata workflow
Keep `tool_choice: "auto"` for both workflows, add a system prompt line requiring a tool call, and retry any response that returns only text
Set `tool_choice: "any"` for the mixed workflow, and force `extract_metadata` by name on the first turn of the metadata workflow
Set `tool_choice: "any"` for both workflows, and list `extract_metadata` first in the tools array so the model selects it before enrichment
correct_answer: Set `tool_choice: "any"` for the mixed workflow, and force `extract_metadata` by name on the first turn of the metadata workflow
explanation: Task 2.3 lists the `tool_choice` options. `"any"` guarantees that the model calls a tool while still letting it pick the right extraction schema for an unknown document type. Forced selection with `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` guarantees that a specific tool runs first, with enrichment in follow-up turns. Forcing `extract_invoice` misroutes receipts and contracts, and `"any"` alone does not guarantee `extract_metadata` goes first. Keeping `"auto"` with a prompt line and retries treats the symptom. Tool order in the array is not a selection rule.

text: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system extracts fields from unstructured documents with `tool_use` and JSON schemas for downstream systems. Your validation-retry loop resends each failed extraction with the document, the failed output, and the specific validation error. Retries fix most date-format errors on the first attempt. Contracts that only say "rates per the attached Schedule B," which you do not receive, fail validation on `hourly_rate` on all three retries. What should you do about these contracts?
options: Stop retrying these cases, return `hourly_rate` as null with a note that it depends on a missing document, and route them for review
Raise the retry limit to five for these contracts, and include a few-shot example showing a correctly extracted hourly rate in the retry prompt
Add the full validation error history from all previous attempts to each new retry, so Claude can see every value that was rejected before
Switch the retry step to a larger model with extended thinking, since the smaller model may be overlooking the rate in long contracts
correct_answer: Stop retrying these cases, return `hourly_rate` as null with a note that it depends on a missing document, and route them for review
explanation: Task 4.4 separates retries that can succeed (format or structural errors) from retries that cannot, because the required information is absent from the source document. The rate lives in Schedule B, which the system never receives, so no amount of retrying can produce it. The right move is to return null, record why, and route the contract for review. More retries, a fuller error history, and a stronger model all assume the answer is somewhere in the document. Pushing harder for a value that is not there invites a fabricated rate.

text: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system extracts fields from unstructured documents with `tool_use` and JSON schemas for downstream systems. A nightly Message Batches API run of 4,000 documents returns 120 errored results, all for documents that exceeded the context limit. Separately, the business now requires each document to be extracted within 30 hours of arrival, and documents arrive around the clock. Which TWO decisions are correct?
options: Resubmit the whole 4,000-document batch with a larger `max_tokens`, and keep one nightly batch since 24-hour processing fits within 30 hours
Resubmit only the 120 failed documents by `custom_id` after chunking them, and keep one nightly batch since processing finishes within 24 hours
Resubmit the whole batch after chunking every document, and submit a new batch every 4 hours so no document waits past the SLA
Resubmit only the 120 failed documents by `custom_id` after chunking them, and submit a new batch at least every 4 hours
correct_answer: Resubmit only the 120 failed documents by `custom_id` after chunking them, and submit a new batch at least every 4 hours
explanation: Task 4.5 covers both decisions. Failed requests are identified by `custom_id` and only those are resubmitted, with a fix that matches the cause: chunking documents that exceeded the context limit. The batch window is up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee. With one nightly batch, a document that arrives just after submission waits almost a day before it is even submitted, then up to 24 more hours, which breaks a 30-hour SLA. Submitting every 4 hours caps total time near 28 hours. Resubmitting all 4,000 documents repeats 3,880 successes, and `max_tokens` limits output length, not input size.

text: Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. Your system extracts fields from unstructured documents with `tool_use` and JSON schemas for downstream systems. Your pipeline reports 97% field-level accuracy on a validation set of mixed invoices, receipts, and customs forms. Customs forms are 4% of volume. Leadership proposes removing human review for every extraction with model confidence above 0.9. What should you do before reducing review?
options: Approve the change since 97% exceeds the target, and lower the auto-approve threshold to 0.8 once a month of results looks stable
Measure accuracy by document type and field, and keep stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to catch new error patterns
Approve the change for invoices and receipts, and route only customs forms to review, since rarer document types usually have lower accuracy
Recalibrate the 0.9 threshold against the validation set's overall accuracy, then remove review for every extraction above the new threshold
correct_answer: Measure accuracy by document type and field, and keep stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to catch new error patterns
explanation: Task 5.5 warns that an aggregate figure like 97% can hide poor performance on a specific document type or field, especially one that is only 4% of volume. Before automating, validate accuracy by document type and field, and keep stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to measure ongoing error rates and catch novel patterns. Approving on the aggregate skips the segment check. Exempting customs forms assumes which segment is weak instead of measuring it. Calibrating against overall accuracy repeats the masking problem at the threshold level.
